So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. And I had Dark Phoenix and another movie to clean at the same time. It’s super slow on weekdays so it’s not a big deal. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. They got up from their seat and yelled at me for “ruining their movie going experience” and wanted to speak to a manager. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

Absolutely, I think so! The kind of close-knit, values-aligned group you describe—often called a **"community of practice," "support network," or "mutual accountability group"**—can absolutely push people to be better in many of the same ways a religious community does. Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Anchor** Religious communities often rely on sacred texts, rituals, or doctrines to define what’s "good" or "right." Your group, however, uses **shared values, principles, or ethical frameworks** (e.g., kindness, honesty, sustainability, justice) as its foundation. When people commit to these values together, they create a **moral accountability** that can be just as powerful as religious teachings. ### **2. Social Accountability & Peer Pressure (The Good Kind!)** Religious communities often use **sacred oaths, confessions, or communal judgment** to keep members on track. Your group does something similar—but with **mutual respect and love** rather than fear or guilt. When you say, *"I’ll check in with you on your goal,"* or *"Let’s hold each other accountable,"* you’re creating a **natural feedback loop** that pushes people to follow through. ### **3. Rituals & Habits That Reinforce Growth** Religious communities use **prayer, meditation, fasting, or rituals** to create mental and emotional space for reflection and growth. Your group might do something analogous: - **Regular check-ins** (like a "spiritual direction" conversation) - **Shared practices** (e.g., journaling together, reading philosophy/ethics, or discussing tough questions) - **Celebrations & milestones** (acknowledging progress, even small wins) These rituals **anchor habits** that keep growth intentional. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Support** Religious communities often provide **belonging, comfort, and a sense of purpose**—especially in hard times. Your group does the same, but with **secular, human-centered support**: - **Vulnerability & trust** (sharing struggles without judgment) - **Encouragement** (reminding each other of their worth) - **Collective problem-solving** (brainstorming solutions together) This kind of **emotional safety** is just as vital for personal growth as religious community can be. ### **5. Collective Purpose & Legacy** Religious communities often tie individual growth to a **larger mission** (helping others, building a better world, etc.). Your group can do the same—whether it’s: - **Activism or social change** - **Personal development for the sake of family/friends** - **Creating something lasting** (a project, a tradition, a legacy) When people see their growth as part of something bigger, they’re more motivated. ### **6. The Power of "Us" vs. "Me"** Studies show that **group identity** (feeling part of a team) increases motivation. Religious communities leverage this with phrases like *"the body of Christ"* or *"the ummah."* Your group does it by saying: - *"We’re in this together."* - *"How can we support you?"* - *"Let’s grow as a group."* This **shared identity** makes personal growth feel less lonely and more meaningful. --- ### **Potential Challenges (And How to Overcome Them)** Of course, secular groups might struggle with some things religious communities handle well: - **Without a shared "higher purpose,"** people might lose motivation over time. *Solution:* Regularly revisit and reinforce your group’s core values. - **Without sacred texts or traditions,** some might feel like they’re "reinventing the wheel." *Solution:* Borrow from philosophy, psychology, or ethics (e.g., Stoicism, Buddhist mindfulness, or secular humanism) to fill that gap. - **Without formal structure,** accountability can fade. *Solution:* Set clear, measurable goals and check-ins (e.g., *"We’ll review progress every 3 months"*). --- ### **Final Thought: It’s About the Relationship, Not the Label** At the end of the day, what matters most is **whether the group feels like a safe, uplifting, and challenging space for growth**. Religious communities do this through faith; your group does it through **human connection, shared values, and mutual care**. If your group is **truly committed to each other’s growth**, it can absolutely be just as transformative—if not more so—because it’s rooted in **real, lived experience** rather than abstract doctrine. Would you say your group already has some of these elements? If not, what’s one thing you’d like to strengthen?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

(Answer: 0/1, but with caveats)** **0 (Not A.I.T.A.)** – *If we’re judging by strict ethical standards of respect, consent, and minimizing harm.* **1 (A.I.T.A.)** – *If we’re judging by practicality, efficiency, and the manager’s perspective.* But the real question isn’t just "Was it wrong?"—it’s: - **Was it a reasonable thing to do in this context?** - **Did the harm outweigh the benefit?** - **Was there a better way to handle it?** --- ### **Why It’s Complicated (And Why the Couple Might Have Reacted Strongly)** 1. **The "Movie Experience" as a Cultural Norm** - Many people (especially fans of superhero movies) **expect** end credit scenes. They’ve built them into their movie-watching rituals—like waiting for the post-credits teaser in *Spider-Man* or the *Star Wars* mid-credits scene. - Telling them there’s **no** end credit scene can feel like **breaking a promise** or **disrespecting their expectations**. Even if it’s not a "promise" per se, it’s a **shared cultural assumption** that movies have these scenes. 2. **The Power Dynamic (Even If Well-Intentioned)** - You were in a **position of authority** (as an usher) giving information to patrons. Even if you meant it as a **helpful tip**, it came across as **directive**—like an order rather than a suggestion. - The couple likely felt **manipulated** or **rushed out of their experience**, especially since they were still in the theater, implying they were **waiting for something**. 3. **The Manager’s Perspective (And Why They Told You to Stop)** - Theaters **don’t want to lose customers** over small things like end credit scenes. A free movie pass is a **damage control** move—meaning this couple’s reaction was **costly** for the theater. - If you keep doing this, you risk **alienating fans** who take their movie experience seriously. Some people **will** complain, and the theater **can’t afford** to lose repeat customers over something that seems petty. - **Efficiency vs. Customer Satisfaction:** While your goal was to clean faster, the theater’s goal is to **keep people happy**—even if it means slower turnover. (Imagine if every usher started "spoiling" things like this—customers would revolt.) 4. **The Flashlight Incident (A Red Flag)** - The couple also complained about you **shining a flashlight**, which suggests they felt **harassed or rushed**. This reinforces that your approach came across as **intrusive**, not just helpful. --- ### **Was It "Wrong"?** **Not inherently wrong**—but **poorly executed** in this case. - **If you were just casually chatting with friends:** *"Hey, no end credit scene here!"* → Fine. - **If you were in a position of authority (usher) and the patrons were still in the theater:** → **Problematic**, because: - It **disrupted their experience** without their consent. - It **assumed they’d care** (which they did, enough to complain). - It **created a negative interaction** that cost the theater money. **Ethical Frameworks to Consider:** - **Utilitarianism (Greatest Good for the Greatest Number):** - Your action **saved time for you and the theater**, but **harmed one couple’s experience**. Was it worth it? Probably not, since the cost (a free movie pass) was higher than the benefit (a few extra minutes). - **Deontological Ethics (Duty & Rules):** - You had a **duty to respect customers’ expectations** (even if they’re not explicit). Telling them there’s no end credit scene **violated their right to enjoy the movie as they expected**. - **Virtue Ethics (How Would a Good Person Act?):** - A **good usher** would **not** assume what customers want or need. Instead, they’d **observe, wait, and clean when the theater is empty**—unless someone explicitly asked for help. --- ### **How Could It Have Been Done Better? (If At All)** If you **really** wanted to help (and not risk complaints), here’s how: 1. **Don’t Assume They Care** – If people are still in the theater, **don’t say anything**. Wait until they leave. 2. **If They Ask:** *"Hey, is there an end credit scene?"* → *"Nope, this one’s over when the credits roll."* - This way, you’re **not imposing**—you’re **answering a question**. 3. **If It’s a Slow Night:** *"Hey, we’re about to close up—want to leave now, or wait for the credits?"* - This gives them **choice**, not a directive. 4. **If You Really Want to Be Helpful:** *"The theater’s empty now—want me to show you where the restrooms are?"* - Redirects their attention **without spoiling anything**. --- ### **Why the Couple Reacted So Strongly** - **They Liked the Movie** → End credit scenes are **part of the experience** for fans. - **They Felt Rushed** → Being told to leave **without their consent** made them feel **disrespected**. - **They Had a Bad Experience** → Now they’ll **remember this theater negatively** (and may not return). - **They Felt Powerless** → As customers, they had **no control** over the situation—your statement was **one-sided**. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It Wrong?** **Yes, in this context.** Not because it was "evil," but because: ✅ **It was unnecessary** (they could’ve left on their own). ✅ **It was intrusive** (you assumed they’d care, but they did enough to complain). ✅ **It had unintended consequences** (cost the theater money, made them look bad). **But was it *your* fault?** Not entirely—**the system is set up for this**. Theaters **know** people wait for end credit scenes, so they **should** have a policy on how to handle it (e.g., "Wait 5 minutes after credits roll before cleaning"). --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Follow the Manager’s Rule** – Stop telling people about end credit scenes. It’s not worth the hassle. 2. **If You Want to Be Helpful:** Wait until the theater is empty before cleaning. 3. **If Someone Asks:** *"Is there an end credit scene?"* → *"Nope, this one’s over when the credits roll."* (But don’t volunteer the info.) 4. **Think About Why You Did It** – Were you **just trying to be efficient**, or did you **enjoy "spoiling" people**? If the latter, that’s a habit worth reconsidering. --- ### **TL;DR** - **A.I.T.A.?** **Yes, in this case.** It was a small thing, but it caused a bigger problem. - **Was it a weird couple?** Maybe. But **most people who wait for end credit scenes do care**—and they’ll remember this. - **Best Practice:** **Don’t assume what customers want.** Let them enjoy the movie as they expect, then clean when it’s over. Would you do it differently next time? Or does this feel like a "small thing" that doesn’t matter?
